subject: botany
question_text: Give the salient features and importance of chrysophytes.

verification.note: Sourced from the Junior Fastrack botany book, Biological Classification chapter (book pp.4-5), which prints the question and a model answer but NO star ranks and NO year citations. Only ONE source book is held for botany — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no botany board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are both STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE for this card, not merely pending: 'not checked' must never be read as 'checked and clean'. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. The book prints 'Given the salient features...' — a grammar slip for Give. It also lists only diatoms as the example; the syllabus group includes desmids (golden algae), which this card adds.

steps.label: Group and habitat
lines: They occur in fresh water as well as
They are microscopic and float passively
steps.why: Placing the group first — which organisms, where they live, how they float — frames the features that follow. (The book lists only diatoms; the syllabus group also includes the desmids, called golden algae.)
common_mistakes: Writing chrysophytes as only diatoms. Desmids (golden algae) belong here too.
Calling them large algae. They are microscopic plankton.
steps.memory_tip: Chrysophytes = diatoms + desmids; fresh and marine; planktonic.
steps.margin_note: Members, habitat and the word plankton in the opening lines.

steps.label: Cell wall
lines: In diatoms the cell wall forms two thin
overlapping shells — the epitheca over the
hypotheca — fitting as a soap box.
The walls are embedded with silica
steps.why: The soap-box wall is the identifying feature of diatoms, and the silica in it explains why the walls survive after the cell dies.
common_mistakes: Swapping epitheca and hypotheca. Epi- means upon, so it is the upper shell.
Writing cellulose in place of silica.
steps.memory_tip: Two shells, one lid: epitheca upon hypotheca, hardened with silica.
steps.margin_note: Shell names, soap box and silica — the three marked terms.

steps.label: Diatomaceous earth
lines: Diatom walls left behind over billions of
This gritty soil is used in polishing and
in the filtration of oils and syrups.
steps.why: Because the silica walls do not decay, they accumulate on the sea floor; the deposit and its uses are the economic importance the question asks for.
common_mistakes: Writing that living diatoms are used for polishing. It is the wall deposit, diatomaceous earth, that is used.
Forgetting the uses. Polishing and filtration are the marked words.
steps.memory_tip: Dead walls accumulate — diatomaceous earth — polishing and filtration.
steps.margin_note: The deposit name plus its two uses.

steps.label: Producers

lines.text: Diatoms are the chief producers in the oceans.

steps.why: Their photosynthesis feeds ocean food chains, so the syllabus calls diatoms the chief producers in the oceans — the most quoted line of this topic.
common_mistakes: Writing chief producers on land. The claim is about the oceans.
steps.memory_tip: One boxed line to end: chief producers in the oceans.
steps.margin_note: Box this line; it is the standard closing sentence of this answer.

insider_note: The word importance is worth half the marks here — diatomaceous earth with its uses, and the chief-producers line.
